faq.a: Yes; prolonged hypoxia or toxin exposure can progress to necrosis if the insult persists.
faq.q: Can reversible cell injury become irreversible without treatment?

faq.a: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin‑mediated renal blood flow, worsening ischemic injury.
faq.q: Why avoid NSAIDs in patients with acute kidney injury?

faq.a: Rely on focused history, physical exam, and bedside tests (e.g., ultrasound, bedside microscopy).
faq.q: What is the first step if imaging is not available?

exam: A patient with fever, right‑upper‑quadrant pain and a tender liver – what bedside test would you perform first and why? — Perform an abdominal ultrasound to detect abscess or hepatomegaly; it guides need for antibiotics or drainage.

You have a febrile child with a swollen leg, but no radiology; how do you differentiate cellulitis from necrotising fasciitis? — Look for severe pain out of proportion, rapid spread, and systemic toxicity; early surgical consult is essential.

A malaria‑positive patient develops oliguria and rising creatinine – what is the most likely pathology and immediate management? — Acute tubular necrosis from severe malaria; give aggressive IV crystalloids and monitor renal function.

When is it appropriate to start empirical antibiotics in a patient with suspected sepsis in a low‑resource setting? — As soon as sepsis is suspected, after drawing blood cultures, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics like ampicillin‑gentamicin.
How would you stage a tumour when only clinical size is known? — Use the ‘T’ component of TNM: T1 ≤2 cm, T2 >2 cm ≤5 cm, T3 >5 cm, T4 invasion of adjacent structures.
What red‑flag sign in a patient with acute abdomen indicates immediate surgical intervention? — Rigid abdomen with absent bowel sounds and worsening tachycardia suggests perforation or peritonitis.

Why is paracetamol preferred over ibuprofen in a patient with acute hepatitis? — Paracetamol at therapeutic doses is less hepatotoxic than NSAIDs, which can impair renal perfusion and worsen hepatic congestion.

A patient on antitubercular therapy develops a rash; what is your next step? — Assess severity; if mild, continue therapy with antihistamine; if severe (e.g., Stevens‑Johnson), stop offending drug and refer.
ai.title: General Pathology Assessment July 2021
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A concise guide for Year‑4 students to approach general pathology questions in low‑resource settings, focusing on clinical reasoning, key investigations and management.

b: Identify whether a process is reversible or irreversible injury.
Distinguish acute from chronic inflammation by duration and cellular infiltrate.
sections.p: General pathology covers the mechanisms of cell injury, inflammation, necrosis, repair and neoplasia. Diagnosis relies on pattern recognition of clinical signs and basic laboratory findings.

b: Mild: limited cellular change, no organ dysfunction.
Severe: extensive necrosis, organ failure, or systemic inflammatory response.
sections.p: Severity is graded by extent of tissue damage and systemic response. Staging systems (e.g., TNM for tumours) are used when applicable; otherwise use clinical categories such as mild, moderate, severe.

b: Infection – malaria, TB, bacterial sepsis.
Ischaemia – severe anaemia, sickle‑cell crisis.
Toxins – traditional medicines, aflatoxin exposure.
sections.p: Common aetiologies in East African hospitals include infections (malaria, TB, HIV‑related opportunists), toxins (herbal remedies, aflatoxin), hypoxia, and trauma.

b: Acute inflammation – redness, heat, pain, loss of function.
Necrosis – blackened tissue, foul smell, loss of viability.
sections.p: Patients may present with pain, swelling, fever, or organ‑specific dysfunction. Look for systemic signs such as tachycardia, hypotension, or altered mental status indicating severe pathology.
Basic tests guide the distinction between reversible injury, inflammation and necrosis, and help stage disease when advanced imaging is unavailable.

t.b: Is there leukocytosis or anaemia? – Elevated WBC suggests infection/inflammation; low Hb may point to chronic disease or haemolysis.
Are kidneys affected? – Rising creatinine indicates acute tubular injury or systemic hypoperfusion.
Is there evidence of sickle cells or malaria parasites? – Presence confirms haemolytic or parasitic cause of cell injury.
Is there organ enlargement or fluid collection? – Detects abscess, oedema, or tumour mass when CT is unavailable.
What is the pattern of cell death? – Necrosis shows loss of nuclei; apoptosis shows cell shrinkage and apoptotic bodies.

b: Septic shock – hypotension unresponsive to fluids.
Acute renal failure – oliguria with rising creatinine.
Malignant transformation – unexplained weight loss, persistent mass.
sections.p: Rapid progression to organ failure, uncontrolled sepsis, or malignant transformation demand urgent action.

b: Antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin, gentamicin) for bacterial infection – chosen for broad coverage and low cost.
Antimalarials (artesunate, quinine) when malaria is confirmed – rapid parasite clearance.
Fluid resuscitation with crystalloids for hypovolaemia – monitor for pulmonary oedema.
Analgesia with paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs in renal impairment.
Surgical drainage of abscesses when accessible – prevents spread.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then support organ function. Use affordable, widely available drugs and avoid those with high toxicity in low‑resource settings.

b: Repeat CBC and renal panel to ensure recovery.
Vaccination (HBV, pneumococcus) where possible.
Health education on safe medication practices.
sections.p: Re‑evaluate clinical response within 48‑72 h. Prevent recurrence by addressing risk factors such as poor sanitation, untreated HIV, and unsafe herbal use.

b: Cellulitis vs. necrotising fasciitis – fascia pain out of proportion suggests necrotising infection.
Acute tubular necrosis vs. pre‑renal azotaemia – urine sodium helps differentiate.
sections.p: Distinguish general inflammatory injury from specific diseases that mimic it.

b: Normal WBC early in severe malaria – rely on smear.
Creatinine may stay normal until >50 % renal loss – monitor urine output.
sections.p: Certain tests may appear normal early in disease, leading to false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained hypotension, altered consciousness, or rapidly worsening organ dysfunction.
